lead: A closed thin cylinder under internal pressure—a boiler, an LPG cylinder, a water main—has two normal stresses in its wall. Hoop stress σ_h acts around the circumference. Longitudinal stress σ_L acts along the axis. A force balance on a cut half-shell gives σ_h = p d/(2t); a balance on the end cap gives σ_L = p d/(4t). Hoop stress is twice longitudinal stress. This is why a cylindrical pressure vessel splits along a longitudinal seam. Here p is internal pressure, d is internal diameter and t is wall thickness.
prereq: You need Unit 1 for Hooke's law, Poisson's ratio and volumetric strain, and Unit 2 for plane stress and Mohr's circle; 7.6 extends the same strain idea to spheres.

blocks.text: Take t ≤ d/20, that is d/t ≥ 20. Here t is wall thickness and d is internal diameter. Stress is then taken as uniform through the thickness. Some books say d/t of 20 or more. Below that, use 7.7.

Cut the cylinder along a diameter over length L. Pressure p acts on the projected rectangle d × L, giving force p d L. Two wall strips, each of area t L, carry hoop stress σ_h. Balance: 2 σ_h t L = p d L.

blocks.where: p = internal pressure (Pa); d = internal diameter (m); t = wall thickness (m); σ_h = hoop stress (Pa).

blocks.text: For a closed end, cut across the axis. Pressure on the circular end area πd²/4 pushes the cap off. The wall ring of area π d t carries longitudinal stress σ_L. Balance: σ_L π d t = p π d²/4.

blocks.where: σ_L = longitudinal stress (Pa); closed ends assumed; other symbols as above.

blocks.text: Closed ends matter: an open pipe has no pressure thrust on its ends, so no longitudinal pressure stress.
ε_h = (σ_h − ν σ_L) / E,   ε_L = (σ_L − ν σ_h) / E
blocks.where: ε_h, ε_L = hoop and longitudinal strain; E = Young's modulus (Pa); ν = Poisson's ratio; σ_h, σ_L as above.

blocks.text: The diameter grows by Δd = ε_h d. The length grows by ΔL = ε_L L; L is cylinder length. The strain route is advanced; only a few universities teach it.

Maximum shear stress through the wall is about σ_h/2. In the wall surface plane it is (σ_h − σ_L)/2 = σ_h/4. Radial stress runs from 0 at the outer surface to −p at the inner surface, so it is ignored.
A riveted or welded shell is weakened at its joint. Use joint efficiency η ≤ 1:

blocks.where: η = joint efficiency (≤ 1); other symbols as above.

blocks.text: The longitudinal joint carries hoop stress, so it usually governs. The sphere in 7.6 has no such split: its stress is p d/(4t) in every direction.

figure.caption: Cutting the shell along a diameter turns pressure into a force p d L, balanced by two wall forces, giving hoop stress; a second cut across the axis balances the end-cap force p πd²/4 against the wall ring πdt, giving longitudinal stress, half the hoop value.

examples.question: A boiler shell has d = 1.2 m, t = 8 mm, p = 1.2 MPa, E = 200 GPa, ν = 0.3. Check the thin-wall limit, find σ_h and σ_L, and the increase in diameter.
examples.answer: d/t = 150, σ_h = 90 MPa, σ_L = 45 MPa, and the diameter increases by 0.459 mm.
examples.check:
p = 1.2e6
d = 1.2
t = 0.008
E = 200e9
nu = 0.3
dt = d / t
sigma_h = p * d / (2 * t)
sigma_L = p * d / (4 * t)
epsilon_h = (sigma_h - nu * sigma_L) / E
delta_d_mm = d * epsilon_h * 1000
print(round(dt, 6))
print(round(sigma_h / 1e6, 6))
print(round(sigma_L / 1e6, 6))
print(round(epsilon_h, 10))
print(round(delta_d_mm, 6))

traps: Substituting the radius value into the diameter formula. σ_h = p d/(2t) needs the diameter; σ_h = p r/t with r = d/2 gives the same number, so using r where d is written halves your answer and is easy to miss. Write the formula and the value with the same symbol.
Setting σ_L = σ_h. Closed ends give σ_L = σ_h/2; an open pipe gives zero.
Mixing p in MPa with d in metres and t in millimetres. Convert all lengths to one unit.
Forgetting joint efficiency η: σ_h = p d/(2tη), with η ≤ 1.
Taking σ_h/2 as in-surface shear. Surface maximum shear is σ_h/4; σ_h/2 is through the wall.

quiz.q: State the thin-wall limit in terms of d and t.
quiz.a: d/t ≥ 20, or t ≤ d/20; stress is uniform through the thickness.

quiz.q: Why is hoop stress twice longitudinal stress?
quiz.a: Hoop stress balances pressure on projected area dL with two wall strips. Longitudinal stress balances end-cap force on πd²/4 with ring area πdt.

quiz.q: A cylinder has d = 0.5 m, t = 5 mm, p = 2 MPa. Find σ_h and σ_L.
A cylinder splits along a longitudinal seam. Which stress caused it?
quiz.a: Hoop stress σ_h. The seam runs along the axis, and hoop stress pulls the two sides of that seam apart.

quiz.q: A welded shell has p = 1 MPa, d = 1 m, t = 10 mm, η = 0.8. Find σ_h.
What does the closed-end assumption do for σ_L?
quiz.a: It gives σ_L = p d/(4t). Without end caps, longitudinal pressure stress is zero.

beyond: Not for the exam. Pressure-vessel codes turn these formulas into wall-thickness rules with corrosion allowance, joint efficiency and hydrotest pressure. Search 'ASME BPVC Section VIII Div 1 shell thickness' and 'IS 2825 pressure vessel'. Finite-element analysis is used when nozzles, saddles or thick walls break the membrane assumption. The same membrane idea reappears in pipe stress analysis and thin-shell civil structures.
